Chapter 8: Joyful Movement—Reconnecting with the Body Through Activity
Now that you’ve built a foundation of body respect, it’s time to look at movement in a whole new way. What if moving your body wasn’t about burning off what you ate, or changing the way you look? Imagine if it was actually about joy—about energy, connection, and just feeling good in your own skin.
For so many of us, exercise has been tangled up with guilt or pressure. Maybe you’ve felt like you needed to “earn” your food, or you’ve avoided movement altogether because it just felt like punishment.
But intuitive eating invites us to try something different: moving our bodies in ways that are enjoyable and meaningful, for reasons that have nothing to do with appearance.
Joyful movement is all about tuning in to what your body actually wants. This could look like dancing around your living room, taking a slow stroll outside, digging into the garden, swimming, or simply stretching with some yoga.
The idea is to notice how movement feels—are you more energized, in a better mood, maybe a little more relaxed or connected? Forget counting calories or tracking every step. It’s about how you feel, not some number on a screen.
Here are a few gentle ways you can explore joyful movement:
First, try asking yourself, “What kind of movement sounds good today?” Maybe you want something gentle. Or maybe you crave something a bit more lively. Would you rather be alone, or do you want to move with others?
Next, pay attention to the sensations in your body during and after you move. Do you feel a little lighter, more energized, or just more at ease?
It also helps to let go of all those rigid exercise rules you might’ve picked up over the years. Give yourself permission to rest, and be flexible. Movement isn’t about perfection—it’s about celebrating those small moments, even if it’s just a couple minutes here and there.
Here’s a helpful way to think about it: imagine movement as play, not a chore. Remember how kids move around just for the fun of it? Adults can do that, too—we can rediscover what makes us feel delight and satisfaction.
You’ll find plenty of real-world stories that show how this works. Maybe you know someone who always forced themselves to run, even though they hated every second. But then, they tried hiking out in nature and suddenly, movement became something they looked forward to. Or maybe someone who avoided exercise for years because of shame, only to find pure joy in a group dance class where the only goal was to have fun, not to perform.
In the end, joyful movement is about building a positive relationship with your body—one step at a time. It’s all about listening, experimenting, and honoring what actually feels good to you.
